name: Herniated Disc
seo_title: Herniated Disc Treatment in North Palm Beach | First Rehab
seo_desc: Herniated or bulging disc in your lower back? One-on-one physical therapy in North Palm Beach to ease pain and rebuild core strength. Medicare accepted.
lede: Physical therapy for a herniated or bulging disc in the lower back, focused on easing nerve pain and getting you back to bending, lifting and moving with confidence.
what_it_is: Between each pair of bones in your spine sits a disc with a tough outer ring and a soft, gel-like center. These discs act like shock absorbers when you walk, run or jump. A herniation happens when part of the soft center pushes through a tear in the outer ring. According to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, the displaced material can press on nearby nerve roots and release chemicals that inflame them.

In the lower back, the discs between L4 and L5 and between L5 and S1 account for about 95% of herniations in adults aged 25 to 55, according to StatPearls. The same reference reports 5 to 20 new cases per 1,000 adults each year, mostly between ages 30 and 50, with men affected about twice as often as women. Age-related drying of the discs makes them less flexible and more likely to tear.
symptoms: Low back pain, often the first thing you notice
Sharp, shooting pain from the buttock down the back of one leg
Numbness or tingling in the leg or foot
Weakness in leg or foot muscles
Pain that worsens with sitting, bending or certain movements
Stiffness that makes it hard to bend or straighten up
causes: Age-related loss of water in the discs, which makes them less flexible
Lifting with the back instead of the legs, especially while twisting
Repetitive straining at work or in sports
Long hours of driving or sitting
A fall or other injury to the back

how_therapy_helps.intro: Most lumbar disc herniations improve without surgery. StatPearls reports that over 85% of acute herniated disc symptoms resolve within 8 to 12 weeks with conservative management. The 2021 JOSPT low back pain guideline supports exercise training, including trunk strengthening, endurance and specific trunk muscle activation, for back pain with leg pain. The APTA ChoosePT herniated disk guide describes a plan built around pain reduction, posture, flexibility, core strength and safe body mechanics for daily tasks.
methods: Early in care, your therapist looks for positions and movements that reduce leg symptoms so you can stay active while the irritated nerve calms down.
Progressive work for the deep abdominal, back and hip muscles helps the spine handle sitting, standing and lifting with less irritation.
Gentle stretching and range of motion work restores movement in the lower back and hips that pain has limited.
You practice bending, lifting, carrying and getting in and out of the car in ways that ease strain on the healing disc.
As pain settles, your program builds staying power for work, exercise and longer days on your feet.

first_visit: Plan on about an hour. Your therapist starts with questions about how the pain began, where it travels and which positions make it better or worse. Testing covers lower back movement, muscle strength and tightness, numbness, reflexes, joint stiffness, posture and walking. Your therapist watches how leg symptoms respond as you move, which guides the first exercises. You begin treatment the same day and go home with a written program.
recovery: Timelines vary with the size of the herniation, how long symptoms have been present and your general health. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons states that most patients are free of symptoms by 3 to 4 months. Cleveland Clinic notes that many people feel better within about a month of conservative care. StatPearls adds that about 30% of patients still have some back pain a year later, so ongoing exercise and good lifting habits remain worthwhile after formal therapy ends.
self_care: Rest for a day or two if needed, then return to gentle movement
Notice which positions ease your leg pain and use them through the day
Avoid heavy lifting and bending while twisting
Change positions often instead of sitting for long stretches
Try ice or heat on your lower back for comfort
see_a_doctor: Loss of bladder or bowel control (a medical emergency called cauda equina syndrome)
Numbness in the groin or inner thighs
Tingling, numbness or weakness that is getting steadily worse
Difficulty standing or walking because of leg weakness
Back pain after a significant fall or accident

faqs.q: Can a herniated disc heal on its own?
faqs.a: Many do improve without surgery. StatPearls, a National Library of Medicine reference, reports that over 85% of acute herniated disc symptoms resolve within 8 to 12 weeks with conservative care such as activity changes, medication from your physician and physical therapy. Improvement is more likely when you stay gently active. A physical therapist can guide which movements to use while symptoms settle.

faqs.q: Is a bulging disc the same as a herniated disc?
faqs.a: The terms are often used interchangeably, and Cleveland Clinic lists bulging disk among the other names for a herniated disk. On imaging reports, however, radiologists frequently describe a bulge and a herniation or protrusion as separate findings. Either can be present without pain, so the report alone does not decide treatment. Your symptoms and exam matter more.

faqs.q: Why does my MRI show a disc bulge if I have no pain there?
faqs.a: Disc changes are very common in people without back pain. A 2015 systematic review in the American Journal of Neuroradiology found disc bulges on imaging in 30% of pain-free 20-year-olds and 84% of pain-free 80-year-olds. The authors concluded that many of these findings may be part of normal aging. That is why therapists match imaging to your actual symptoms.

faqs.q: Will I need surgery for a herniated disc?
faqs.a: Most people do not. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons recommends trying nonsurgical treatment such as physical therapy first, and surgery is generally considered when symptoms persist despite that care or when nerve weakness is progressing. Loss of bladder or bowel control is different: it is an emergency and needs immediate medical attention.

faqs.q: Can a herniated disc happen again?
faqs.a: It can. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons notes that after surgery there is up to a 20 to 25% chance the disc will herniate again during your lifetime. Without surgery, the APTA ChoosePT guide points to habits that lower strain on the spine, including good posture, safe lifting, a healthy weight, not smoking and staying physically active.

faqs.q: Can physical therapy make a herniated disc worse?
faqs.a: A good program is adjusted to how your symptoms respond. Your therapist checks how leg pain, numbness and strength change as you move and exercise, and changes the plan if symptoms spread farther down the leg or get worse. Some soreness from new exercise can happen, but increasing leg numbness or weakness should be reported to your therapist and physician right away.

signOrSymptom: numbness or tingling in the leg

notes_for_reviewer: ICD-10 M51.26 (Other intervertebral disc displacement, lumbar region) verified as billable on icd10data.com. Herniation with radiculopathy would instead be M51.16; confirm which the clinic prefers to show.
StatPearls gives two different figures (over 85% resolve within 8 to 12 weeks, and 90% after 6 weeks). Only the 85% figure is used.

Bulging disc is treated as a related term per assignment. Cleveland Clinic uses it interchangeably; the FAQ notes radiology reports often separate bulge from herniation/protrusion (the Brinjikji review reports them separately). Clinician should confirm the wording.
AAOS recommends 1 to 2 days of rest; self-care tip mirrors that.

'Coughing or sneezing' dropped from symptoms (Mayo's wording on that refers to neck/arm pain).
